title: Waiting for a community occupational therapist with arthritis: what to do in the meantime (UK guide)

direct_answer: Waits for a community occupational therapist (OT) can be long. While you wait, ring the team to check you are on the list and tell them if anything changes, especially falls or no longer managing to wash, dress or use the toilet, as they may see you sooner. Ask your council for a needs assessment if you need help with care. Meanwhile, make the riskiest jobs safer: wash sitting down, use a perching stool in the kitchen, keep things at waist height and get a night light. Simple aids such as a raised toilet seat or tap turners can be bought, but get advice before buying anything costly or fitted. Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself.

content:
If you have been referred to a community occupational therapist (OT) and are still waiting, you do not have to just sit tight. You can check your place in the queue, tell the team if things get worse, make the hardest daily tasks safer now and get some simple equipment yourself.

This guide is for people with arthritis waiting for an OT home visit, and for family who help. To understand what an OT does and how referral works, see occupational therapy for arthritis. If you also need help with care, such as washing or meals, ask for a social care needs assessment.

Check the referral and how to chase it

  • Ring the team that is due to see you (usually the council adult social care team or the NHS community therapy team) and check they have your referral and the right phone number.
  • Ask roughly how long the wait is and how they decide who is seen first.
  • Keep a short note of the date, who you spoke to and what they said.
  • If you cannot get through, ask your GP surgery or whoever referred you to chase it.

Tell them if things change

Teams usually see people sooner when risk is higher. Ring back and explain clearly if you:

  • have a fall or a near-fall
  • can no longer get in or out of bed, a chair, the bath or the toilet safely
  • can no longer wash, dress or make a hot drink
  • are a carer who can no longer manage, or have hurt yourself helping
  • are about to come home from hospital

Make the hardest jobs safer now

Washing

If getting in and out of the bath is hard, do not risk it. Strip wash at the sink sitting on a stool or chair until you have been assessed. Use a non-slip mat and keep the room warm.

Toilet

A raised toilet seat or a free-standing frame can make standing easier. See toilet frames.

Chairs and bed

Use a firm chair with arms. Avoid low, soft sofas. A cushion can raise a seat a little. For bed and chair tips, see safer transfers with hip and knee osteoarthritis.

Kitchen

Sit on a perching stool to prepare food, use a trolley to carry things, fill the kettle with a jug and move things you use every day to between waist and shoulder height. See kitchen adaptations.

At night

A plug-in night light and a clear path to the toilet reduce the risk of falls.

Simple aids you can buy yourself

Small aids such as tap turners, jar openers, long-handled sponges, sock aids, grab handles that do not need drilling and raised toilet seats are widely sold. Living Made Easy and its AskSARA tool give impartial advice to help you choose. You may not have to pay VAT on equipment for a long-term condition.

Before you buy anything costly, fixed to the wall or for the bath, stairs or bed, wait for advice or ask the team. Fitted grab rails, stair rails and bigger adaptations may be provided free, and some can be funded through a Disabled Facilities Grant.

Other help while you wait

  • Your GP can review your pain relief and refer you to physiotherapy.
  • Your pharmacist can help with packaging and medicines that are hard to open.
  • Some people pay for a private OT assessment. If you do, ask for a written report you can share with the council.
  • If you need care, the council needs assessment is free, whatever your income.

When to see your GP or get urgent help

See your GP if pain or stiffness is getting worse, you are having falls or you are struggling to cope. Ask NHS 111 or your GP for same-day advice if a joint becomes hot, red and swollen, or you feel unwell with a fever. Call 999 if someone has fallen and cannot get up, is badly hurt or has hit their head and is drowsy.

For carers and family

Write down what you are doing to help and what is getting harder: this is useful evidence when you chase the OT team. Ask the council for a carer’s assessment for yourself.

Common questions

How long is the wait for a community OT?

It depends on where you live and how urgent your needs are. Ask your local team.

Can I refer myself to an OT?

In many areas you can contact your council’s adult social care team directly and ask for an OT assessment.

Will I have to pay for equipment?

Equipment assessed as needed by the council or NHS is often provided free on loan. Ask the team what applies where you live.
